intro_html:
As of 23 September 2026 Governor Newsom has neither signed nor vetoed SB 868. If he does nothing by 30 September it becomes law without his signature, and either way it would take effect on 1 January 2027. The enrolled text covers municipal utilities as well as PG&E, SCE and SDG&E, which matters in Los Angeles: the city is served by LADWP, a city department, not Southern California Edison. Two limits are easy to miss. The exemption covers only a device certified as a complete plug-in system, and as of September 2026 no complete system has been certified to UL 3700, the standard written for them (what that means). And the bill says nothing about landlords, tenants or associations.

For condo owners, Civil Code §714 voids association rules that “effectively prohibit or restrict” a solar energy system. But unless the declaration says otherwise, §4145 makes a balcony “exclusive use common area”, and §714.1 lets an association limit systems in common areas to those it approves. What §714 guarantees is process: the decision must be in writing, and an application not denied within 45 days is deemed approved.

The 32.9¢ state average below blends investor-owned and municipal utilities. LADWP’s standard R-1A rate charges 24.4 to 27.3¢ per kWh in its first tier in 2026 and 30.2 to 33.2¢ in its second, before tax, and a kWh a panel displaces comes off the highest tier a household reaches. balco.nyc’s calculator takes the rate from your own bill for a specific Los Angeles address.

faq: Would SB 868 apply to LADWP customers in Los Angeles?

Yes, if it becomes law. The enrolled bill exempts qualifying plug-in devices from the interconnection rules of local publicly owned utilities such as LADWP as well as investor-owned utilities, and bars either from requiring approval, fees or extra equipment, though a utility may ask for a simple online registration. It would take effect on 1 January 2027, and the exemption lapses on 1 January 2030 unless the Legislature extends it.
Can a California condo association stop a balcony solar panel?

It can require approval. Civil Code §714 voids association rules that effectively prohibit or restrict a solar energy system, but a balcony is exclusive use common area unless the declaration says otherwise (§4145), and §714.1 lets an association limit systems in common areas to those it approves. The association must decide in writing, and an application it has not denied within 45 days is deemed approved. This summarizes the statutes and is not legal advice.
